Modern.brandNameRationale: Three words, one concept. Night & Day names the two halves of hospitality service. The brand sits on the fact that the hotel runs continuously, the staff change shifts, and the guest gets the same standard from both. Plain, modern, slightly poetic.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern hotel brands are competing on design, food, and local credibility. The chain model is being challenged by independent houses with stronger personalities. The customer wants a hotel that feels owned, not operated.

Modern.tagline: Modern hotels with the warmth of a guest room.

Modern.manifesto: Modern hotels have started to feel like apartments designed by a committee. Stay Over is a small group of properties run on the opposite premise — the room is set up the way an experienced host's guest room would be set up, with the things you forgot and the things you wished for. The brand is the guest room, not the lobby.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern boutique hotels have converged on a single aesthetic — soft modernism, plant, low lighting. The market is over-served on style and under-served on warmth. There is room for a brand that competes on hosting craft, not interior design.
Modern.competitorLandscape: ACE Hotel (acehotel.com) defined the modern boutique. Standard (standardhotels.com) holds the playful slot. Citizen M (citizenm.com) sits in the modern-functional position. We compete on hosting feel — closer to a friend's guest room than a designer's lobby.
Modern.positioningStatement: Stay Over is a small group of modern hotels run with the warmth of a well-prepared guest room.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Two words, one location. Stonebridge sounds like a real English country estate. Hall is the architectural word for the large central room of such an estate. Together it reads as a heritage house that has been receiving guests since the 1800s.
Luxury.story: Stonebridge began as a private country house held by the same family for four generations. The current generation decided to open it to a small number of guests, a few weeks each year. The house is the brand. We have not added to it. We have not subtracted from it.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end hospitality has been moving toward larger destinations and bigger spa programs. There's a parallel market for slower, smaller country house hotels. The customer is paying for restraint, real walking distance to the next thing, and silence.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Babington House (babingtonhouse.co.uk) sits in the closest peer group. Cliveden House (clivedenhouse.co.uk) is the institutional reference. Heckfield Place (heckfieldplace.com) is the contemporary peer. We are quieter than all of them.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small country house that takes a limited number of guests each year.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy. Often inherited. Spends weekends in the country. Books the same house every year. Values the staff knowing the family's names without being told.

dos: Address the guest by surname
Send paper invitations to the seasonal openings
Speak in the language of stewardship, not service

Luxury.story: The Calder is a fourteen-room property in a converted nineteenth-century house, run by a small permanent team. The same family has owned it for three generations. Most guests are repeat guests. The house is closed for two weeks every January for maintenance.
Luxury.industrySummary: Premium hotel groups have grown into recognizable cohorts. There is a quieter market for single-property houses — fourteen to thirty rooms, single ownership, no signage, run with the discretion of a private residence.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: The Connaught (the-connaught.co.uk) sets the bar for old-house luxury. Aman (aman.com) holds the modern peer position. The Newt (thenewtinsomerset.com) is the country-house reference. We belong with single-property houses, not with collections.
Luxury.positioningStatement: The Calder is a single property, run as a house — fourteen rooms, one team, one family.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not expand. The product is the singular building. The renewal is the relationship with the staff, not the visit to a brand.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Three words, two objects. Room & Key names the entire hospitality offer in its smallest form. The brand strips away spa, gym, lobby, mini-bar, and concierge. The guest gets a room and a key. Plain and honest.
Minimal.industrySummary: Hotel brands keep adding features and selling them as amenities. There's an opening for a brand that subtracts. One good room. One key. Clean sheets. Hot water. No talking.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most hotel brands compete on amenities. We compete on absence. The closest peers are some Japanese ryokan and the early Yotel airport rooms. There is no direct competitor in this position at scale.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Hotels that sell you a room and a key. Nothing else.

Corporate.industrySummary: Hospitality investment and management is a serious B2B category. Hotel owners, real estate investors, and institutional landlords need operators they can trust to run properties on their behalf. The category is mostly served by giant chains and a few specialist firms.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Lockhart is a surname with an operational, slightly Scottish register. Hospitality Group signals the category and the holding structure. Reads as a portfolio operator with several properties under management, not a single brand.
Corporate.manifesto: Lockhart operates a portfolio of mid-market hotels and serviced apartments. The buyer is an institutional owner or a family office holding the real estate. We run the front-of-house and the operations under a single management contract. The properties keep their own names; we keep them full.
Corporate.industrySummary: Hotel ownership and operation are increasingly separated. Owners hold the real estate; operators run the property. The mid-market has consolidated around a few large brand operators; the opening is for a serious mid-vendor with operational depth and discretion.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Aimbridge Hospitality (aimbridgehospitality.com) is the U.S. reference. Interstate (interstatehotels.com) is the peer. HighGate (highgate.com) sits in the institutional-operator slot. We belong in the regional mid-market operator category.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Lockhart Hospitality Group is a regional management company operating mid-market hotels and serviced apartments under owner-held brands.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Owners outsource operations to us; the property keeps its identity. We compete on operational metrics — RevPAR, GOP, payroll efficiency — not on brand glamor.

Creative.tagline: A hotel for the night staff who run it.
Creative.brandNameRationale: The Hour references the night manager's watch — the working hours of hotel operations. The definite article + Hotel suffix follows the considered-creative hospitality naming school.
Creative.manifesto: Most hotel brands sell the lobby. We sell the night. The strange request at 2 a.m. The conversation at the front desk with the only other person awake. The corridor at 4 a.m. when the cleaners haven't started. Night Manager is the hotel brand for people who keep odd hours and want a hotel that does too.
Creative.industrySummary: Hotel brand has been polished and daylight-only for too long. The customer who travels for fun, stays up late, and wants a hotel with personality hasn't been served by a single brand cleanly. There's room for one.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Ace Hotel (acehotel.com) has the cultural side. The Standard (standardhotels.com) does the irreverent posture well. CitizenM (citizenm.com) holds the playful affordable end. Generator Hostels (staygenerator.com) sits in the social-budget tier. We are louder than all of them with sharper voice.
Creative.positioningStatement: A hotel brand for people who travel for the night, not the day.

Creative.tagline: A hotel brand built around the night.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Bedwell is a real but uncommon English surname meaning 'beside the well' — historically associated with rest. Hotels is the plain category suffix. Single-surname + plain category follows the considered boutique-hotel school (Ace, Standard, Wythe).
Creative.manifesto: We started Good Night because the entire job of a hotel is the night. The lobby is decoration. The brand is decoration. The night is the product. Every room is set up around one promise — that the guest sleeps well. The pillow, the blackout, the temperature, the silence. The rest is window dressing.
Creative.industrySummary: Hotel brands have over-invested in lobbies, daytime amenities, and rooftop bars. Sleep, the actual product, is treated as a baseline. There is a real opening for a brand that takes the opposite view and competes on night quality.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Equinox Hotels (equinox-hotels.com) touches the wellness-sleep narrative. Six Senses (sixsenses.com) holds the high-end wellness slot. Westin Heavenly Bed marketing was the first to claim the sleep position. We are sharper and more singular — the sleep is the brand, not the amenity.
Creative.positioningStatement: Good Night is a hotel brand built entirely around the night — the pillow, the silence, the temperature.
Creative.positioningRationale: Every decision in every property is measured against one metric: did the guest sleep well? The lobby exists to support the night. The brand voice exists to support the night.

targetAudience.primary: Travelers 30–55 who are tired and notice the difference a good night makes.
behaviors: Pack their own pillow.
Read reviews for noise and blackout.
Travel for work more than they want to.
Wake early.
motivations: Want a hotel that takes sleep seriously.
Want a dark, quiet room and good bedding.
Want to wake feeling like they slept.

dos: Talk about pillows, blackout, temperature, by spec.
Write the welcome note as a goodnight note.
Send a thank-you email the morning after, not a survey.
Use the brand line — 'Good night' — wherever a sign-off is needed.
donts: No daytime-amenity messaging in the brand voice.

messagingPillars.name: Engineered for night
messagingPillars.description: Triple-glazed windows, blackout to 99.5%, room temperature held within half a degree, mattress and pillow specified per room. Published specs.

messagingPillars.name: The goodnight note
messagingPillars.description: Every guest gets a handwritten goodnight note on the pillow with the manager's first name. The morning email asks one question: did you sleep?

messagingPillars.name: Day is secondary
messagingPillars.description: We do not run a destination restaurant. The lobby is a corridor. The hotel exists for the night and is honest about that.

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark — Bedwell Hotels set in a quiet display serif, with a tiny crescent mark instead of an apostrophe. Reads as a sign-off, not a brand.

colorPalette.name: Lamp
colorPalette.meaning: Accent — the color of the bedside lamp left on.

colorPalette.name: Linen
colorPalette.meaning: Page and sheets — an honest off-white.

typography.primary: A quiet display serif for the wordmark and welcome notes.
typography.secondary: A modern grotesque for working type and signage.
typography.rationale: The serif speaks. The sans labels. Most of the brand surface is unlit.

Creative.brandDescription: Good Night is a hotel brand built entirely around the night — the pillow, the silence, the temperature.
Creative.mission: Every decision in every property is measured against one metric: did the guest sleep well? The lobby exists to support the night. The brand voice exists to support the night.
coreValues: Warm — we are friendly, not formal.
Specific — generalities are how people avoid commitment.
Considered — we choose fewer things, more carefully.
Quiet — restraint is the loudest thing in a noisy room.

Bedwell Hotels works across:
